Gastroschisis

Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons

Definition

Gastro means GIT tract, schisis means splitting or separating

Gastroschisis is a congenital abdominal wall defect, there is a full thickness hole in the abdominal wall at which the infant’s abdominal organs herniate

the hole mostly located on the right of the umbilicus

herniated organs has no cover, they have direct contact with external environment

Most commonly organs herniating through this hole are intestine, stomach and liver

Must be differentiated from omphalocele (this is explained a little bit later in the gastroschisis vs omphalocele chapter of this video)

Epidemiology

Gastroschisis incidence is 1 in 2500 live births and it is increasing every decade

10% of cases are associated with anomalies outside GI tract

Gastroschisis infants have high risk of intrauterine growth restriction 60% thus greater risk for preterm labor too

Risk of preterm delivery in gastroschisis 25% in comparison with normal babies 5%

Gastroschises survival rate is 90% with treatment, 0% without treatment

Pathophysiology

Pathophysiology of gastroschisis is related to embryonic folding

Embryonic folding is the process by which the fetus converts from flat sheet of cells, into a tube like structure and it start at 4 weeks

Embryonic folding has to be complete for the abdominal wall to close , if not then gastroschisis occurs

OpenStax College, CC BY 3.0 <https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/3.0>, via Wikimedia Commons

This is caused by inadequate blood supply due to right umbilical artery premature regression (normally right umbilical artery stays longer until it regress while in gastroschisis it regress prematurely)

So there is not enough blood going to the abdominal wall and this lead to Gastroschisis which is hole in the right side of the abdominal wall that allows intestine to protrude through it

Intestine get irritated and inflamed when exposed to amniotic fluid

This lead to reduced bowel motility and absorption because of the irritation

Herniated bowel may have compromised vascular supply which lead to impaired bowel development

Complications: Intestinal stenosis, short bowel, intestinal atresia, perforation, necrosis, volvulus or GIT infections can occur

Causes

Cause unknown

But there is risk factors

Risk factors

Young maternal age < 20 years

Maternal low body mass index

Maternal use of salicylates like aspirin

Maternal genitourinary infection during first trimester

Maternal cigarette smoking or alcohol or illicit drug use

Gross appearance

Defect to the right of the umbilical cord insertion site, smooth edges and it is usually less than 4 cm in diameter

The defect is separated from the base of umbilical cord by small bridge of skin

Intestine are thickened with no overlying membrane

Gastroschisis vs omphalocele

Omphalocele is when the intestine protrudes into the umbilical cord and it stay sealed by the umbilical cord which protect it from the amniotic fluid while in gastroschisis there is no cover

Variants of gastroschisis

Closed or vanishing gastroschisis: abdominal wall defect has closed before birth => blood supply to the herniated bowel is impaired now => herniated bowel is now ischemic and necrosis occur

Left sided gastroschisis (rare): the only difference is that the defect is to the left of the umbilicus

Diagnosis

Gastroschisis can be diagnosed at the end of the first trimester by ultrasound, because the physiological return of intestine should be complete by 11 weeks of gestation if not then it is gastroschisis

US shows multiple loops of bowel floating freely in the amniotic fluid, bowel herniation is seen on the right of the umbilical cord insertion

Gastroschisis can be differentiated from omphalocele by US too, in gastroschisis there is lack of membranous covering of the bowel

In Omphalocele there is high probability of CVS, and genitourinary anomalies while in Gastroschisis there is low probability for GIT, CNS, CVS, MSK and genitourinary anomalies

Some of those anomalies can be identified by US too

Injury to the herniated bowel from exposure to the amniotic fluid or contracture of the umbilical ring is common

The injury also can be identified by US, features include: dilatation of the bowel, loss of peristaltic activity, changes in bowel wall echogenicity, alterations in mesenteric blood flow and changes in stomach position

Maternal alpha fetoprotein levels are elevated too

Delivery of gastroschisis baby

Vaginal delivery is possible with all gastroschisis cases unless the liver is herniated then C section delivery has to be done

Resuscitation

After delivery of gastroschisis newborn, ventilation or intubation might be needed

NG decompression tube should be inserted and IV access obtained

If there is bowel congestion, try to look for any kinking and relieve by repositioning of the bowel

Bolus IV normal saline 20 ml/kg after delivery is obligatory to substitute the third space fluid loss and insensible fluid losses, sometimes 80 ml/kg is needed initially

Initial dose of ampicillin and gentamicin shortly after delivery to prevent GIT infections

Parenteral nutrition is very important in gastroschisis and should be used until bowel function goes back to normal

Treatment

The goal is to return the intestine back to the abdominal cavity and slowly introduce feeding to the baby

The two main options of treatment are

primary closure

staged closure with the use of a temporary silo and progressive reduction

Silo is a clear, sterile plastic or silicone bag that is placed over the exposed organs for putting pressure for gradual reduction and also the silo is effective in protection and preventing fluid loss

Primary closure

this procedure include reduction of the bowel back to the abdominal cavity and closing the defect

This procedure done quickly after birth as an attempt to return the herniated organs back to their place, if failed then silo method is done

Failure of primary closure is when

Intestine can’t be placed back into the abdominal cavity (not enough space)

Intestine can be placed but the intraabdominal pressure is higher than 10mmHg

Central venous pressure is greater than 4 mmHg when bowel placed back

Staged closure using silo

This method developed in the 1990s

This method start by applying silo (plastic or silicon bag) in the delivery room, after application the bowel is reduced gradually back into the abdominal cavity

Silo positioned around the opening without the need for sutures or anesthesia

Adewale O. Oyinloye1*, Auwal M. Abubakar1, Samuel Wabada2 and Lateef O. Oyebanji1, CC BY 4.0 <https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0>, via Wikimedia Commons

Bowel viability is assessed continuously while in silo to ensure no impairment in the blood supply

This process takes between 1 and 14 days until bowel is reduced, and then definitive closure is done which is similar to the primary closure

Intestinal atresia

Sometimes gastroschisis is associated with intestinal atresia

Intestinal atresia has to be anastomosed again

Post operative care

Ensure there are no effects from increased abdominal pressure (e.g. abnormal ventilation, decreased renal function, GIT ischemia), if abdominal compartment syndrome is suspected then laparotomy and silo placement should be performed

In Gastroschisis bowel function is decreased (motility and absorption are affected), and it gradually improves in most patients

No enteral feeding in gastroschisis until bowel function returns, during that time NG decompression, parenteral nutrition are required

When bowel activity returns, enteral feeding started gradually until enteral feeding is enough and that is when the patient can be discharged, this can take from 1 to 2 months
